question: As a matter of general national real estate practice (not a Georgia-specific statutory rule), is a real estate commission rate ever fixed or set by law, an MLS, or a trade association?
choice_a: Yes -- state law nationally sets a standard commission percentage that all brokers must charge
choice_b: Yes -- the local MLS sets a binding minimum commission rate for all its members
choice_c: No -- commission rates are a matter of negotiation between broker and client; fixing or coordinating commission rates among competing brokers, MLSs, or associations raises antitrust concerns and is not a legally set rate
choice_d: Yes -- national trade associations are legally authorized to set a uniform commission schedule
explanation: As a matter of well-established national practice and antitrust doctrine, real estate commission rates are negotiable between broker and client and are never fixed by law, an MLS, or a trade association -- coordinated rate-setting among competing brokerages raises antitrust concerns rather than reflecting a lawful fixed schedule.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate commission practice and antitrust doctrine

question: As a matter of general national real estate practice, what does 'procuring cause' refer to in a commission dispute between two cooperating brokers?
choice_a: The broker who happened to hold the earnest money at closing, regardless of any other involvement
choice_b: The broker who first printed a promotional flyer for the listing
choice_c: A concept that applies only to for-sale-by-owner transactions, never to MLS-cooperated sales
choice_d: The broker (or brokers) whose uninterrupted efforts were the direct cause of the buyer and seller reaching an agreement, a concept used to help determine which broker is entitled to a commission when more than one broker was involved with a buyer or property
explanation: Procuring cause is a general national real estate concept (commonly arbitrated through MLS/association procedures rather than set by Georgia statute) describing the broker whose uninterrupted efforts directly brought about the buyer-seller agreement -- used to resolve commission disputes when multiple brokers had contact with the same buyer or property.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate commission-dispute doctrine

question: As a matter of general national real estate practice, how are listing-side and selling-side (buyer-side) commission splits typically established between the two cooperating brokerages on a transaction?
choice_a: By agreement between the brokerages -- commonly documented through the listing broker's offer of cooperation and compensation to buyer brokers, rather than being set by any statute
choice_b: By a fixed statutory percentage split that applies uniformly to every transaction nationwide
choice_c: The split is always mandated to be exactly 50/50 by federal law
choice_d: GREC sets the split percentage for every Georgia transaction by rule
explanation: Commission splits between a listing brokerage and a cooperating buyer's brokerage are a matter of agreement between the brokerages -- commonly documented in the listing broker's offer of compensation -- rather than a percentage fixed by statute or by GREC rule.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate commission practice

question: As a matter of current, widely adopted national real estate practice (following industry-wide changes to buyer-representation practices), what has become standard regarding a written agreement between a buyer and their buyer's agent before touring homes?
choice_a: Written buyer-representation agreements remain optional everywhere in the United States, with no practice change of any kind
choice_b: A written buyer-representation agreement specifying the buyer agent's compensation terms is now widely required before a buyer tours a home with an agent, reflecting industry-wide practice changes -- though the specific Georgia-mandated form and timing were not independently re-verified this session
choice_c: Buyer agents are now prohibited nationwide from receiving any compensation whatsoever
choice_d: Only sellers, never buyers, may now enter into a written representation agreement
explanation: Following industry-wide changes to buyer-representation practices, a written buyer-representation agreement addressing compensation terms has become standard practice before touring homes with a buyer's agent -- a significant shift from prior practice, though this session did not independently re-verify Georgia-specific implementation details such as a mandated GREC or GAR form.
source_note: hedge: current national real estate industry practice; Georgia-specific implementation details not independently re-verified this session

question: A qualifying broker wants to pay a departing licensee's final commission check to the licensee's newly formed unlicensed LLC rather than to the licensee personally, without meeting any of the narrow O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(17) carve-outs (such as the more-than-20%-owned entity provision). Is this permissible?
choice_a: Yes -- a broker may always redirect a licensee's commission to any entity the licensee names
choice_b: Yes, as long as the LLC is formed in Georgia rather than another state
choice_c: No -- absent satisfying one of the narrow statutory carve-outs, paying compensation for licensed activity to an unlicensed entity is an unfair trade practice under § 43-40-25(b)(17)
choice_d: Yes, as long as the licensee signs a one-page waiver form
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(17) generally prohibits paying compensation for licensed activity to an unlicensed person or entity, subject only to narrow enumerated carve-outs (such as the more-than-20%-owned-entity provision) -- simply naming an unlicensed LLC does not itself satisfy those carve-outs.

question: A salesperson's affiliation with Broker A ends on June 1, and she affiliates with Broker B on June 5, having personally delivered her transfer application to GREC that same day. A sale she had been working on for Broker A closes on June 20, but no written agreement was reached between Broker A and Broker B about that pending transaction under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-19(c). Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(c)(5), which broker is entitled to the compensation earned at that June 20 closing?
choice_a: Broker A -- compensation always follows whichever broker the licensee was affiliated with when the listing or buyer relationship first began
choice_b: Neither broker -- the compensation is forfeited entirely without a written agreement
choice_c: The compensation must be split automatically 50/50 between Broker A and Broker B whenever no written agreement exists
choice_d: Broker B -- absent a documented § 43-40-19(c) agreement covering the pending transaction, compensation eligibility follows the firm the licensee's license was assigned to when the compensation was earned (at the June 20 closing), which is Broker B
explanation: Without a documented § 43-40-19(c) agreement, § 43-40-18(c)(5) ties compensation eligibility to which firm the license was assigned to when the compensation was actually earned (at closing) -- here, Broker B, even though the transaction originated under Broker A.

question: As a matter of general national terminology (not itself a defined Georgia statutory term), what does a 'dual variable rate commission' (DVRC) generally refer to, and what does it require?
choice_a: A listing arrangement in which the seller has agreed to pay a different commission rate depending on whether the buyer is represented by the listing broker (in-house) or by a cooperating outside broker -- generally understood, under national fair-practice norms, to require disclosure to the seller and, before showing property to a prospective buyer, to that buyer as well
choice_b: A commission structure that automatically doubles once a deal exceeds $1 million in price
choice_c: A rate that varies based solely on the buyer's credit score
choice_d: A federally mandated flat commission rate applicable to every dual-agency transaction nationwide
explanation: A dual variable rate commission (DVRC) describes a listing arrangement where the commission rate differs depending on whether the buyer is represented in-house or by an outside cooperating broker; general national fair-practice norms call for disclosure of this variable arrangement to the seller and to a prospective buyer before showing the property, since an undisclosed DVRC can create an incentive conflict for the showing agent.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate commission-disclosure terminology

question: Under general national listing-agreement doctrine, how does an 'open listing' typically affect which broker earns a commission?
choice_a: An open listing always guarantees the first broker who signed the listing a commission, regardless of who procures the buyer
choice_b: The seller may list with multiple brokers simultaneously, and only the broker who is the procuring cause of an accepted sale earns a commission; if the seller sells the property personally without any broker's efforts, no commission is owed to any broker
choice_c: An open listing legally requires the seller to use only one broker at a time
choice_d: An open listing is identical in every respect to an exclusive-right-to-sell listing
explanation: Under an open listing, a seller may engage multiple brokers at once, and only the broker whose efforts actually procure the sale (or who is the procuring cause) earns a commission -- if the seller sells the property without any broker's involvement, typically no commission is owed under an open listing.

question: Under general national listing-agreement doctrine, how does an 'exclusive-right-to-sell' listing differ from an 'exclusive-agency' listing with respect to commission entitlement?
choice_a: The two listing types are functionally identical and always produce the same commission outcome
choice_b: An exclusive-agency listing always pays a higher commission rate than an exclusive-right-to-sell listing
choice_c: Under an exclusive-right-to-sell listing, the listing broker earns a commission no matter who procures the buyer -- including the seller personally; under an exclusive-agency listing, the broker earns a commission if any broker (including themselves) procures the buyer, but the seller retains the right to sell personally without owing a commission
choice_d: Only an exclusive-agency listing permits cooperation with other brokers through the MLS
explanation: An exclusive-right-to-sell listing entitles the listing broker to a commission regardless of who ultimately procures the buyer, even the seller personally. An exclusive-agency listing entitles the broker to a commission if any broker procures the sale, but preserves the seller's right to sell the property personally without triggering a commission obligation to the listing broker.

question: Under general national brokerage-commission doctrine, once a broker produces a ready, willing, and able buyer on the seller's stated listing terms, is the broker's commission generally considered earned even if the sale never actually closes because the seller refuses to complete the transaction?
choice_a: No -- a broker is never entitled to any compensation unless the sale actually closes, regardless of circumstances
choice_b: No -- the buyer, not the seller, becomes personally liable for the broker's commission in this situation
choice_c: Yes, but only if the buyer defaults, never if the seller defaults
choice_d: Generally, yes -- under traditional brokerage doctrine, a broker who procures a ready, willing, and able buyer on the seller's terms has fully performed and generally earns the commission, even if the seller then wrongfully refuses to complete the sale (subject to the specific terms of the listing agreement)
explanation: Under traditional national brokerage doctrine, producing a ready, willing, and able buyer on the seller's stated terms generally completes the broker's performance and earns the commission -- a seller who then wrongfully refuses to close does not defeat the broker's earned right to compensation, though the specific listing agreement's language controls the details.

question: As a matter of general contract practice, when a buyer defaults on a purchase and the earnest money is forfeited to the seller as liquidated damages, how is the broker's commission on that forfeited amount typically handled?
choice_a: The disposition is a matter of the specific purchase agreement's and listing agreement's terms -- many contracts specify a division of forfeited earnest money between the seller and the broker(s), often up to the amount of the commission that would have been earned had the sale closed
choice_b: The broker automatically keeps 100% of the forfeited earnest money regardless of the contract's terms
choice_c: The broker is never entitled to any share of forfeited earnest money under any circumstances
choice_d: State law nationally mandates the earnest money always be split exactly 50/50 between broker and seller with no contract override
explanation: How forfeited earnest money is divided between seller and broker(s) upon a buyer's default is governed by the specific purchase agreement and listing agreement terms -- many standard contracts provide for the broker to receive some portion (often capped at the commission that would have been earned), but this is a matter of contract, not a uniform national rule.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate contract practice

question: What is a 'safety clause' (also called a protection clause, extender clause, or carryover clause) commonly found in a listing agreement, and what does it protect?
choice_a: A clause insuring the property against physical damage during the listing period
choice_b: A clause entitling the listing broker to a commission if the property is sold within a specified period after the listing expires to a buyer the broker had introduced to the property (or otherwise procured) during the listing term, protecting the broker from a seller circumventing the commission by simply waiting for the listing to expire
choice_c: A clause that automatically renews the listing agreement indefinitely without the seller's consent
choice_d: A clause that voids the listing agreement automatically if the broker is disciplined by GREC
explanation: A safety (protection/extender) clause protects the listing broker's commission if, within a defined post-expiration window, the seller sells to a buyer the broker had procured or introduced during the listing term -- preventing a seller from waiting out the listing's expiration to avoid paying a commission the broker's efforts actually generated.

question: As a matter of general national doctrine, is a real estate commission generally earned by simply holding a license, or must some additional condition be satisfied?
choice_a: Simply holding an active license automatically entitles a licensee to compensation on every closed transaction in their market area
choice_b: A commission is earned automatically the moment a listing agreement is signed, regardless of any subsequent performance
choice_c: A commission is generally earned only when the licensee (through their broker) performs licensed brokerage services under an enforceable agreement, and the specified condition for compensation (e.g., closing, or procuring a ready-willing-able buyer, depending on the agreement's terms) is satisfied -- merely holding a license is not itself sufficient
choice_d: No commission may ever be earned without a fully executed and recorded deed
explanation: A commission is not earned by licensure status alone -- it requires actual performance of brokerage services under an enforceable agreement, with entitlement typically triggered by the specific condition the agreement sets (commonly closing, or procuring a ready, willing, and able buyer), consistent with general national brokerage-commission doctrine.

question: Under general national real estate practice, what is a 'referral fee' in the context of broker-to-broker compensation, and to whom is it typically paid?
choice_a: A fee a buyer pays directly to their own agent for referring them to a mortgage lender
choice_b: A fee that only insurance companies, never real estate brokers, may pay or receive
choice_c: A mandatory fee set by federal statute at exactly 25% of the total commission on every referred transaction
choice_d: A fee paid by a licensed broker to another licensed broker (or, in Georgia, subject to the narrow foreign-referral-agent carve-out, occasionally to an unlicensed foreign referral source) for referring a client, typically calculated as a percentage of the commission ultimately earned on the referred transaction
explanation: A referral fee is compensation paid between licensed brokers for referring a client to one another, typically a percentage of the commission earned on the referred transaction -- Georgia law generally requires the recipient to be licensed, subject only to the narrow foreign-referral-agent carve-out discussed elsewhere in this chapter's compensation rules.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate referral-fee practice

question: As a matter of general national practice, may a real estate brokerage lawfully offer a portion of its commission as a rebate or credit to its OWN client (e.g., the buyer it represents) at closing?
choice_a: Commission rebates to a brokerage's own client are permitted in many states as a matter of general national practice, though the specific permissibility, required disclosures, and any conditions can vary by state and by the terms of the particular transaction and lender guidelines
choice_b: No -- commission rebates to a brokerage's own client are illegal in every U.S. state without exception
choice_c: Rebates are permitted only if paid directly by the seller, never by the buyer's own brokerage
choice_d: Rebates are permitted only for cash purchases with no financing involved
explanation: As a matter of general national practice, many states permit a brokerage to rebate a portion of its earned commission to its own client, though specifics (permissibility, required disclosures, lender/closing treatment) can vary; this reflects general national practice rather than a single uniform nationwide rule, and Georgia-specific rebate mechanics were not independently verified this session.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate commission-rebate practice; Georgia-specific mechanics not independently verified this session
